text: An order went through with zero items. The ticket says the smallest valid order is one.
Open the training checkout in Visual Studio Code, with its terminal connected to the approved workspace.
Run the command on screen from the directory containing the validator and its tests.
Keep that command handy. We will use exactly the same one twice more.
Three tests pass. Read their names with me. They try five, one, and negative one.
Which test would catch an order for zero items?
Try the missing value directly. Import the same public function that the tests use.
Call it with zero and print the return value. There it is. True.
Read the ticket beside that result. An order with zero items must be rejected, so we expected false.
The existing tests can all pass while this particular call gives the wrong answer.
Leave the source as it is for a moment. This is our chance to find out whether a new test can actually detect the defect.
Here is a question you can put to Copilot in Plan mode.
Which expression admits zero, and what will happen if we assert that zero must be rejected?
Include the issue, the validator, and its tests.
Check the prediction yourself on line three. Substitute zero for quantity.
Is zero greater than or equal to zero?
Yes. The equality part is enough to let it through.
Now try one and negative one in your head. One is greater than zero.
Negative one is smaller. The equality at the boundary explains all three outcomes.
Give Agent a small first job. Add one zero regression to the existing test class and leave the validator untouched.
You can also type the two lines shown here.
Read the assertion from the inside out. The function receives zero.
The assertion requires its result to be false.
A test that simply checks whether zero is false would tell us nothing about our validator.
Before running it, inspect the changed file list. You should see the test file alone.
That lets us attribute the next failure to the behavior already present in the starting code.
Run the same command again. First check the total. Four tests ran this time.
Now find the failure and follow it back to the line that calls the validator with zero.
Read the assertion message. True is not false. That is the observation we predicted.
The three earlier cases still pass. Keep this output with the test-only patch.
Suppose the runner had stopped at an import error. What would you know about zero?
Very little. Fix the setup and rerun until the assertion itself executes.
Now the regression can catch the bug. Open the production diff. Remove the equals sign.
The expression now asks whether quantity is strictly greater than zero.
Keep the public function signature and the new assertion as they are.
Make a prediction before the next run. Zero is equal to zero, so the new expression returns false.
Five and one should still pass. Negative one should still be rejected.
Run that saved command a third time. The zero test now passes, and the total is still four.
Compare the failure and the pass side by side. The method name and its assertion are identical.
For a handoff, give your teammate the starting checkout, the test-only diff and its failing output, then the source diff and its passing output.
They can apply the changes in that order and repeat your result.
Try the same method on a separate exercise. An order may contain one through one hundred items, including one hundred.
The draft on screen uses a strict comparison at each end.
Pause the video here. Write the expected answers for ninety-nine, one hundred, and one hundred and one.
Which single regression would expose the mistake before you edit the function?
Ready?
The answers are true, true, and false. The draft rejects exactly one of those valid examples, one hundred.
Write an assertion that accepts one hundred. Watch it fail, then include equality at the upper limit and rerun.
Notice how the ticket decided which way equality belongs.
Reading the rule, testing the edge, and replaying the same check will serve you at either end of a range.
